# Purpose and scope

This guideline documents the FLicc utilities that turn a length-based
catch-curve assessment into a management procedure (MP) for the FLR `mse`
package. It concentrates on **how the modules connect** inside `mp()`, the
**principles behind the indicators** they produce (SPR, Z, `LBIspr`,
`LBImean`), the **harvest control rules** that use them (`lbi.hcr()` and the
new rfb-type rule `rfb.flicc.hcr()`), and the **settings that control run
time and robustness** of the repeated FLicc fits.

The operating model (OM) and the length-sampling observation error model
(OEM) are documented elsewhere and only summarised here:

| Doc | Content | Status |
|-----|---------|--------|
| **mse-01 (this)** | FLicc MP modules: flow, indicators, HCRs, run time, robustness options | prototype |
| mse-02 | Splendid alfonsino length-selective OM (FLRef), `sampling.lfd.oem()` and full FLicc MSE runs | planned (OM in *FLicc_MSE_lite_OM_v3*) |
| mse-03 | Robustness set: misspecified M, Linf, CVL and selectivity form | planned |
| FLRef `lfd-01` | Length-frequency simulation and `sampling.lfd.oem()` | [FLRef docs](https://henning-winker.github.io/FLRef/) |

All single-fit examples below use the `alfonsino` example data in FLicc, so
each function can be run and checked in isolation before it is used inside
`mp()`.

# The flow of an FLicc management procedure

## Modules and what they pass on

`mp()` calls three user modules in every management cycle: an estimator
(`est`), a harvest control rule (`hcr`) and an implementation system
(`isys`). The OEM in front of them is called by `mp()` itself.

```
OM (FLom)                  true N, F, M; catch by gear from partial F
  |
  |  sampling.lfd.oem()     (FLRef) two-stage length samples by gear and year,
  v                         reported catch by gear with error
attr(stk, "lfd")            FLQuants: len x year x unit x ... x iter, one per gear
attr(stk, "catch_gear")     FLQuants: catch by gear (shares are formed in flicc.sa)
  |
  |  est  = flicc.sa()      one fiticc() fit per iteration (loop or parallel),
  v                         diagnostics, usable iterations, indicators
ind                         FLQuants: LBIspr.<gear>, LBImean.<gear>, [pooled],
  |                         SPR, Z, Ztgt, Zrel   (NA for unusable iterations)
  |  hcr  = lbi.hcr()  or  rfb.flicc.hcr()
  v
ctrl                        fwdControl holding a TAC *multiplier* (not a TAC)
  |                         decision.hcr flag in tracking
  |  isys = flicc.is()      TAC_y = TAC_{y-1} x mult, change limits, Cmax,
  v                         optional split across units (areas)
ctrl                        fwdControl with the TAC for ay + management_lag
  |
  |  fwd.om()               projection
  v
OM
```

Two design decisions run through all modules:

1. **The length data travel as attributes of the observed stock.** `mp()`
   only passes `stk` and `idx` to the estimator, so `sampling.lfd.oem()`
   attaches the samples as `attr(stk, "lfd")` and `attr(stk, "catch_gear")`,
   and `flicc.sa()` reads them from there. `stk` itself is returned
   unchanged.
2. **The HCRs return a relative change, not an absolute catch.** FLicc has no
   biomass scale, so the HCR returns a multiplier on the previous TAC and
   `flicc.is()` converts it. Every iteration that cannot be assessed (failed,
   non-converged or boundary fit) carries `NA` indicators, which the HCRs turn
   into `mult = 1` (TAC unchanged).

| Module | `mp()` slot | Reads | Returns | Tracks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sampling.lfd.oem()` (FLRef) | `oem` | OM stock, gear objects, common random numbers | `stk` with `lfd`, `catch_gear` attributes | |
| `flicc.sa()` | `est` | `attr(stk, "lfd")`, `attr(stk, "catch_gear")` | `ind` (indicators, year x iter) | `conv.est`, `sprbound.est`, `refit.est`, `used.est`, `Lref.<gear>`, `Lmeanref.<gear>` |
| `lbi.hcr()` | `hcr` | `ind[[gear]]`, `ind$SPR` | multiplier | `trend.hcr`, `metric.hcr`, `decision.hcr`, `mult.hcr` |
| `rfb.flicc.hcr()` | `hcr` | `ind[[index]]`, `ind[[f]]`, `ind$SPR` | multiplier | `r.hcr`, `f.hcr`, `b.hcr`, `mult.hcr`, `decision.hcr` |
| `flicc.is()` | `isys` | multiplier, previous TAC, `decision.hcr` | TAC for `ay + management_lag` | `tac.is` |

## Timing within a cycle

With the usual `mse` arguments (`iy`, `fy`, `y0`, `data_lag`,
`management_lag`, `frq`):

* the assessment year is `ay`; the last data year is `dy = ay - data_lag`;
* `flicc.sa()` fits the length data from `y0` to `dy`, or only the last
  `nyrs` years up to `dy` (rolling window, Section 7);
* `flicc.is()` sets the TAC for `ay + management_lag`, starting from `initac`
  in the first cycle (`ay == iy`) and from the TAC tracked at `ay - frq`
  afterwards;
* with `frq > 1` the TAC is held between assessments, and the trend windows
  `n1`, `n2` of the HCRs refer to *data years*, not to cycles.

# The estimator: `flicc.sa()`

## Inputs from the OEM

1. **Length compositions.** `attr(stk, "lfd")` is summed over units
   (`unitSums()`), so area- or sex-structured samples are pooled into one
   composition per gear. Each gear-year composition is then rescaled to the
   effective sample size `ess.g` with `lfdess()`. The OEM's own sample size
   (`ess_len`, typically hundreds of fish) would give the multinomial or
   Dirichlet-multinomial likelihood far too much weight relative to the
   real information in a length sample; `ess.g` (default 150) sets the
   weight explicitly and can differ by gear. `ess.g = NULL` keeps the sampled
   counts.
2. **Catch split.** Catch shares by gear and year are formed from
   `attr(stk, "catch_gear")` (catch weight by gear, with reporting error), so
   that the partition carries observation error and differs by iteration and
   cycle. `catch_by_gear` is only a fallback for an OEM that does not attach
   catch by gear.
3. **Life history.** `lhpar` (Linf, k, M or M/k, L50, a, b) is static across
   cycles and builds the length template with `stocklen()` for each
   iteration's composition.

The OEM must deliver **annual** compositions (`season = FALSE` in
`sampling.lfd.oem()`); seasonal samples are not pooled by `flicc.sa()`.

## One fit per iteration

`fiticc()` fits one FLR iteration at a time, so `flicc.sa()` loops over
`args$it`. Each iteration gets its own `stocklen()` template and catch
shares, and `fiticc()` is called with the `settings` list (population and
observation model, CVL, priors, robustness options; see `?fiticc`).

The loop runs sequentially or in parallel through `foreach`/`doFuture`
(`parallel = TRUE`, `workers`). The two levels of parallelism must never be
active together: if `mp()` itself runs in parallel, set
`outer_parallel = TRUE`, which forces `parallel = FALSE` inside `flicc.sa()`.
A `future::multisession` plan opened inside every `mp()` worker is a nested
backend and crashes workers.

## Diagnostics and usable iterations

Each fit is classified before any indicator is computed:

| Check | Setting | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Fit fails (`try-error`) | | not used |
| Convergence (`need_refit_flicc()`: optimiser code, finite objective, positive-definite Hessian) | `drop_nonconv = TRUE` | not used if not converged |
| SPR at the boundary (any year with SPR $\geq$ `spr_max`) | `spr_max = 0.99` | flagged, not used |
| Rescue of boundary fits with another selectivity form | `refit_sel_fun` | refit kept only if it leaves the boundary |
| Inputs of boundary fits | `debug_dir` | saved as `flicc_bound_ay<year>.rds` |

Boundary solutions (SPR close to one, i.e. F close to zero) arise mostly when
a dome-shaped selectivity can explain the absence of large fish by a steep
descending limb instead of mortality. `refit_sel_fun = c("logistic",
"logistic")` retries such fits with asymptotic selectivity.

An unusable iteration gets `NA` for all indicators in that cycle; the HCRs
keep its TAC (`mult = 1`). The proportion of usable fits (`used.est` in the
tracking) should be monitored: a management procedure that is frequently
"frozen" by failed fits performs differently from the one that was intended.

## Indicators returned in `ind`

| Element | Definition | Equals 1 at |
|---|---|---|
| `LBIspr.<gear>` | $P^{obs}(L \geq L_{ref}) / P^{ref}(L \geq L_{ref})$ (Section 4.2) | SPR target |
| `LBImean.<gear>` | $\bar L^{obs} / \bar L^{ref}$ (Section 4.3) | F = M (default) or SPR target |
| `LBIspr`, `LBImean` | weighted mean over gears (`pool` not `"none"`) | as above |
| `SPR` | fitted SPR (0–1) | |
| `Z` | $F_{ap} + M$ (apical F, fitted M) | |
| `Ztgt` | $F_{SPR_x} + M$ | |
| `Zrel` | $Z / Z_{tgt}$ | SPR target (> 1: fishing above target) |

`pool` decides how gear indices are combined: `"none"` (default, per gear
only), `"equal"`, `"catch"` (reported catch shares by year), or a named
vector of weights. Catch weighting is not necessarily best: a gear that
selects large fish responds more strongly to changes in survival than a gear
that catches mostly recruits, even if its catch is smaller.

The tracking also stores the reference lengths `Lref.<gear>` and
`Lmeanref.<gear>` of every refit, so drift of the references between cycles
(e.g. through re-estimated selectivity) can be seen directly.

# Indicators: principles

The examples use one FLicc fit to the alfonsino data with a dome-shaped and
an asymptotic gear.

```{r example-fit}
data("alfonsino")
lfd <- FLQuantLen(lfd_long_to_wide(as.data.frame(lfd_alfonsino)),
                  unit = "cm", midL = FALSE)
lhpar <- FLPar(linf = 55.7, k = 0.08, M = 0.162, L50 = 31.1859,
               a = 0.004721956 / 1000, b = 3.146168)
stklen <- stocklen(lfd, lhpar, m_model = "constant")

gears   <- names(lfd)
sel_fun <- c("dsnormal", "logistic")
cbg     <- c(0.7, 0.3)
settings <- list(pop_model = "gtg", obs_model = "dm", CVL = 0.1,
                 prior_sigmaF = c(log(0.5), 0.3, 1), spr_ref = 40)

t_fit <- system.time(
  fit <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                settings = settings)
)[["elapsed"]]
gears
```

## SPR, Z and Zrel

SPR is the fitted spawning potential ratio by year. The mortality indicators
compare total mortality with the mortality at the SPR target:

$$
Z_y = F_{ap,y} + M, \qquad Z_{tgt} = F_{SPR_x} + M, \qquad
Z^{rel}_y = Z_y / Z_{tgt}.
$$

$F_{SPR_x}$ is the apical F that gives SPR = x % under the fitted selectivity,
growth and M. Because `settings$spr_ref` equals the target (default 40), it
is taken from `fit$report$Fspr` without any further calculation (Section 7.1).

```{r spr-z}
M    <- c(fit$report$lhpar["M"])
Z    <- fit$report$Fap + M
Ztgt <- fspr_flicc(fit, spr = 40) + M
round(rbind(SPR = c(fit$report$spr), Zrel = c(Z / Ztgt)), 3)
```

## `LBIspr`: proportion of large fish relative to the SPR target

For each gear $g$, the equilibrium numbers-at-length at $F_{SPR_x}$ are
filtered through the gear's fitted selectivity, $v_g(l) = N_l(F_{SPR_x})\,
s_g(l)$. The reference length $L_{ref,g}$ is the length at which the
cumulative vulnerable numbers reach the fraction `thresh` (default 0.75), so
about a quarter of the catch at the target lies above it. The indicator
compares the observed proportion above $L_{ref,g}$ with that expected
proportion:

$$
LBIspr_{g,y} = \frac{\sum_{l \geq L_{ref,g}} C^{obs}_{g,l,y} \big/ \sum_l C^{obs}_{g,l,y}}
                    {\sum_{l \geq L_{ref,g}} v_g(l) \big/ \sum_l v_g(l)} .
$$

Values below one mean fewer large fish than at the target, i.e. fishing
pressure above $F_{SPR_x}$. The reference is gear-specific because the same
stock produces different length compositions in a trawl and a gillnet.

```{r lbispr}
lbi <- LBIspr(fit, spr = 40, thresh = 0.75)
attr(lbi, "Lref")
round(do.call(rbind, lapply(lbi, function(x) c(index(x)))), 3)
```

```{r lbispr-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot_LBIspr(fit, spr = 40, thresh = 0.75)
```

## `LBImean`: mean length relative to Lmean(F = M)

`LBImean()` is the model-based analogue of the ICES length indicator
$f = \bar L / L_{F=M}$. The reference mean length is computed from the same
filtered equilibrium numbers, but at a reference F:

$$
\bar L^{ref}_g = \frac{\sum_{l \geq L_{c,g}} \bar l\, N_l(F_{ref})\, s_g(l)}
                      {\sum_{l \geq L_{c,g}} N_l(F_{ref})\, s_g(l)}, \qquad
LBImean_{g,y} = \bar L^{obs}_{g,y} / \bar L^{ref}_g ,
$$

with $F_{ref} = \text{FM} \times M$ (`ref = "FM"`, default `FM = 1`, i.e.
Lmean at F = M) or $F_{ref} = F_{SPR_x}$ (`ref = "spr"`). The cut-off
$L_{c,g}$ (`lc = "sel50"`) is the first length at which the gear's
selectivity reaches 0.5, which excludes poorly selected small fish as in the
ICES $L_c$ convention.

The ICES approximation $L_{F=M} = (L_\infty + 2 \cdot 1.5\, L_c)/(1 + 2
\cdot 1.5)$ assumes knife-edge selection and a single growth curve.
`LBImean()` instead uses the fitted growth variability (GTG), M and gear
selectivity, including dome-shaped curves, where the ICES formula is not
defined.

```{r lbimean}
lbm  <- LBImean(fit, ref = "FM", FM = 1)
lbms <- LBImean(fit, ref = "spr", spr = 40)
rbind(Lmean_FM = attr(lbm, "Lmean_ref"), Lmean_spr40 = attr(lbms, "Lmean_ref"),
      Lc = attr(lbm, "Lc"))
round(do.call(rbind, lapply(lbm, function(x) c(index(x)))), 3)
```

## Levels and trends

Both length indicators are ratios to a model reference. Their **level**
depends on the model's scale — M, Linf, CVL and the selectivity form all
enter the reference — so a misspecified M shifts every year's value by
roughly the same factor. Their **trend** does not: a constant reference
cancels in a ratio of recent to earlier years,

$$
r = \frac{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{y \in \text{recent}} I_y}
         {\frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{y \in \text{previous}} I_y}
  = \frac{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum \bar L^{obs}_y}{\frac{1}{n_2}\sum \bar L^{obs}_y}
  \quad \text{for } I_y = \bar L^{obs}_y / \bar L^{ref}.
$$

This is the main design principle of the HCRs below: the trend component
(`r`) is robust to the life-history assumptions, while any level component
(`f`, the SPR status, the SPR safeguard `b`) inherits the model's scale bias
and is where the robustness set (mse-03) has to show that the MP is still
precautionary. Between refits the reference can still move when selectivity
or CVL are re-estimated; the tracked `Lref.<gear>` and `Lmeanref.<gear>`
show by how much.

# Harvest control rules

## SPR status rule: `spr_rule()`

`spr_rule()` maps current SPR to a relative change with four triggers: a
fixed reduction `dlow` below `b1`, a linear increase to the no-change
plateau (`dopt`) between `b2` and `b3`, a linear increase to `dhi` at `b4`,
and a fixed increase above `b4`. `plot_hcrspr()` shows the rule with the
stock-status zones (`blim`, `bthr`) and, optionally, the fitted SPR series.

```{r spr-rule, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_hcrspr(b1 = 0.1, b2 = 0.3, b3 = 0.5, b4 = 0.75, blim = 0.1, bthr = 0.2,
            dlow = -0.2, dopt = 0, dup = 0.15, spr_target = 0.4,
            obs = c(fit$report$spr), years = dimnames(fit$report$spr)$year)
```

## Trend and status: `lbi.hcr()`

`lbi.hcr()` combines a trend ratio $r$ on one element of `ind` (recent `n1`
years over the previous `n2`, default 2-over-3) with the SPR status
multiplier $s$ from `spr_rule()`. The status change is applied only when
both point in the same direction:

$$
\text{mult} = \begin{cases} s & \text{if } (r < 1 \text{ and } s < 1)
\text{ or } (r > 1 \text{ and } s > 1)\\ 1 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
$$

The rule does nothing while the stock is in the plateau or while trend and
status disagree, which damps the response to noisy SPR estimates. The size
of the change comes from the level (SPR), only its timing from the trend.
`decision.hcr = 3` is set when SPR falls below `spr_trigger`, which makes
`flicc.is()` apply its change limits (`dtaclow`, `dtacupp`, `Cmax`) in those
iterations.

`hcr_sprlbi()` applies the same logic to a single fit, outside `mp()`:

```{r lbi-hcr}
g <- gears[1]
round(c(trend = r_rule(lbi[[g]], n1 = 2, n2 = 3),
        status = spr_rule(tail(c(fit$report$spr), 1), b1 = 0.1, b2 = 0.3,
                          b3 = 0.5, b4 = 0.75),
        mult = hcr_sprlbi(fit, gear = g, b1 = 0.1, b2 = 0.3, b3 = 0.5,
                          b4 = 0.75)), 3)
```

## The rfb-type rule: `rfb.flicc.hcr()`

`rfb.flicc.hcr()` adapts the ICES category-3 rfb rule to the FLicc
indicators:

$$
A_{y+1} = A_y \; r^{\gamma}\, f\, b\, m .
$$

| Component | `rfb.flicc.hcr()` | ICES rfb | Bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| $r$ trend | ratio of `index` (any element of `ind`), `n1` over `n2`, exponent `gamma` | biomass index, 2-over-3 | cancels (trend) |
| $f$ fishing pressure | `f = NULL` (f = 1, rb rule); `"LBImean"`/`"LBImean.<gear>"` ($\bar L/\bar L_{F=M}$, the ICES-type f); `"LBIspr"`/`"LBIspr.<gear>"`; `"Zrel"` (used as $1/Z^{rel}$) | $\bar L / L_{F=M}$ | inherits level bias |
| $b$ safeguard | $\min(1,\, SPR_y / SPR_{trigger})$, `spr_trigger` (default 0.25), `nspr` years | $\min(1, I_y/I_{trigger})$ | inherits level bias |
| $m$ multiplier | `m` (default 0.95) | 0.95 for $k < 0.2$, 0.90 otherwise | |

The SPR safeguard replaces the biomass-index trigger of the ICES rule, since
no biomass index exists in a length-only MP. It is the only component that
forces a reduction when the stock is depleted but stable. Because recruitment
falls as SPR falls, a given SPR corresponds to a lower biomass ratio
(`flicc2FLStockR(s = )`, `sprbrel_flicc()`), so `spr_trigger` should be
chosen on that scale.

As in the ICES rule, `decision.hcr = 3` when $b = 1$, so the stability
limits in `flicc.is()` (ICES: +20 %, −30 %, i.e. `dtacupp = 1.2`,
`dtaclow = 0.7`) apply only while the safeguard is inactive. Note that this
is the opposite convention to `lbi.hcr()`, where the limits apply *below*
the trigger.

The components can be computed from one fit to see what each choice of `f`
implies:

```{r rfb-components}
rfb_parts <- function(fit, index, f = NULL, n1 = 2, n2 = 3, gamma = 1,
                      spr_trigger = 0.25, m = 0.95) {
  ind <- c(lapply(LBIspr(fit), index), lapply(LBImean(fit), index))
  names(ind) <- c(paste0("LBIspr.", gears), paste0("LBImean.", gears))
  M <- c(fit$report$lhpar["M"])
  ind$Zrel <- (fit$report$Fap + M) / (fspr_flicc(fit, spr = 40) + M)
  I  <- c(ind[[index]])
  r  <- (mean(tail(I, n1)) / mean(head(tail(I, n1 + n2), n2)))^gamma
  fv <- if (is.null(f)) 1 else tail(c(ind[[f]]), 1)
  if (identical(f, "Zrel")) fv <- 1 / fv
  b  <- min(1, tail(c(fit$report$spr), 1) / spr_trigger)
  round(c(r = r, f = fv, b = b, m = m, mult = r * fv * b * m), 3)
}
idx_g <- paste0("LBIspr.", gears[1])
rbind(rb          = rfb_parts(fit, idx_g),
      f_LBImean   = rfb_parts(fit, idx_g, f = paste0("LBImean.", gears[1])),
      f_LBIspr    = rfb_parts(fit, idx_g, f = idx_g),
      f_Zrel      = rfb_parts(fit, idx_g, f = "Zrel"))
```

## Implementation system: `flicc.is()`

`flicc.is()` converts the multiplier into a TAC,
$TAC_y = TAC_{y-1} \times \text{mult}$, for the iterations flagged by
`decision.hcr > 2` limits the change to `dtaclow`–`dtacupp` times the
previous TAC and caps it at `Cmax`, and sets it for `ay + management_lag`.
The first cycle needs `initac`, normally the last observed catch. With
`catch_area` the TAC is split across units (areas) by fixed shares.

# Assembling the management procedure

The OM `om` and the OEM `oem` (with `sampling.lfd.oem()`, `season = FALSE`)
are built in mse-02. Given those, alternative MPs differ only in the `hcr`
element:

```{r mp-ctrl, eval = FALSE}
library(mse)

est <- mseCtrl(method = flicc.sa, args = list(
  lhpar = lhpar, sel_fun = c("dsnormal", "logistic"),
  settings = list(pop_model = "gtg", obs_model = "dm", CVL = 0.1,
                  ngtg = 13, maxsd = 2,
                  prior_sigmaF = c(log(sigmaF_hat), 0.01, 1),  # Section 7.3
                  Lplus = 50, rob_eps = 0.001,                  # Section 8
                  spr_ref = 40),
  spr = 40, thresh = 0.75, ess.g = 150, nyrs = 5,
  lbi = c("spr", "mean"), pool = "none",
  refit_sel_fun = c("logistic", "logistic"),
  n_restart = 1, outer_parallel = TRUE))

isys <- mseCtrl(method = flicc.is, args = list(
  initac = initac, dtaclow = 0.7, dtacupp = 1.2))

hcrs <- list(
  # trend x status
  lbi    = mseCtrl(method = lbi.hcr, args = list(
             gear = "LBIspr.Gillnet", b1 = 0.1, b2 = 0.3, b3 = 0.5, b4 = 0.75,
             dlow = -0.2, dopt = 0, dhi = 0.15, n1 = 2, n2 = 3)),
  # rb: trend and SPR safeguard only
  rb     = mseCtrl(method = rfb.flicc.hcr, args = list(
             index = "LBIspr.Gillnet", spr_trigger = 0.25)),
  # rfb with the ICES-type f = Lmean / Lmean(F = M)
  rfb_Lm = mseCtrl(method = rfb.flicc.hcr, args = list(
             index = "LBIspr.Gillnet", f = "LBImean.Gillnet",
             spr_trigger = 0.25)),
  # rfb with f = Ztgt / Z
  rfb_Z  = mseCtrl(method = rfb.flicc.hcr, args = list(
             index = "LBIspr.Gillnet", f = "Zrel", spr_trigger = 0.25)))

mps <- lapply(hcrs, function(h) mpCtrl(list(est = est, hcr = h, isys = isys)))

mseargs <- list(iy = 2024, fy = 2054, y0 = 2015, data_lag = 1,
                management_lag = 1, frq = 2, it = nsim)

runs <- lapply(mps, function(ctrl)
  mp(om, oem = oem, ctrl = ctrl, args = mseargs, parallel = TRUE))
```

`outer_parallel = TRUE` is set because `mp()` runs in parallel here; with
`parallel = FALSE` in `mp()`, use `parallel = TRUE, workers = n` in
`flicc.sa()` instead. The FLRef OEM currently requires `parallel = FALSE` in
`mp()` (common random numbers are plain arrays that `mp()` does not split
across workers; see the FLRef developer notes), so until that is fixed the
parallel loop belongs inside `flicc.sa()`.

# Run time

Inside `mp()` the cost of a run is approximately

$$
\text{time} \approx n_{cycles} \times \frac{n_{iter} \times
(\bar t_{fit} + \bar t_{ind})}{n_{workers}},
$$

with $n_{cycles} = (fy - iy)/frq$. The indicator time $\bar t_{ind}$ is now
negligible (Section 7.1), so run time is governed by the fit time
$\bar t_{fit}$, which depends on the data window, the model settings and how
often the optimiser restarts. The example fit above took
`r round(t_fit, 2)` s on this machine.

## Reference points computed in TMB (FLicc 1.0.9)

Before 1.0.9, every `LBIspr()` call solved for $F_{SPR_x}$ in R with
`uniroot()`, recomputing the unfished state at each step. The TMB template
now has a per-recruit block that is evaluated only at report time (TMB's
double evaluation, never during optimisation). It computes $F_{SPR_x}$ for
the targets in `settings$spr_ref` and the numbers-at-length at those F, at
the fitted parameters:

* `fspr_flicc()` returns the stored value for these targets (no
  computation); other targets cost one TMB call (`brp_tmb_flicc()`).
* `LBIspr()` takes its reference composition from the stored numbers.
* `LBImean(ref = "FM")` needs `nf_flicc()` at $F = M$, one TMB call.

Keep `settings$spr_ref` equal to the `spr` argument of `flicc.sa()`
(both default to 40). If they differ, every indicator call falls back to
one extra TMB evaluation per iteration.

```{r speed-ref}
c(Fspr40_stored = system.time(fspr_flicc(fit, spr = 40))[["elapsed"]],
  Fspr30_tmb    = system.time(fspr_flicc(fit, spr = 30))[["elapsed"]],
  LBIspr        = system.time(LBIspr(fit))[["elapsed"]],
  LBImean       = system.time(LBImean(fit))[["elapsed"]])
```

## Settings that control fit time

| Setting | Where | Effect on time | Effect on results |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nyrs` | `flicc.sa()` | fixed, short data window instead of a growing `y0:dy`; cost stays constant across cycles | F random walk over fewer years; $\sigma_F$ weakly identified (Section 7.3) |
| `n_restart` | `flicc.sa()` / `fiticc()` | each restart is a full `nlminb()` run; 0–1 is usually enough inside `mp()` | more restarts reduce residual gradients |
| `grad_tol` | `flicc.sa()` / `fiticc()` | restarts stop once the max gradient is below it | also the convergence criterion |
| `obs_model` | `settings` | `"mn"` fastest; `"dm"` adds one parameter | `"dm"` absorbs overdispersion of sampled compositions |
| `ngtg`, `maxsd` | `settings` | cost scales with `ngtg`; little gain beyond 9–13 groups | `maxsd` sets the actual Linf spread and the largest reachable length |
| `ess.g` | `flicc.sa()` | none directly; very large values make the likelihood sharp and convergence harder | weight of the length data |
| `refit_sel_fun` | `flicc.sa()` | one extra fit per boundary iteration | rescues boundary fits |
| `frq` | `mp()` args | halves the number of assessments for `frq = 2` | TAC held between assessments |
| `parallel`, `workers`, `outer_parallel` | `flicc.sa()` / `mp()` | divides by the number of workers; one level only | none |
| `verbose = FALSE` | `flicc.sa()` | avoids console output from every restart | none |

## Estimate $\sigma_F$ once, then fix it

FLicc smooths fishing mortality over years with a random walk on log F by
gear,

$$
\log F_{g,y} \sim N(\log F_{g,y-1},\, \sigma_F^2), \qquad
\log \sigma_F \sim N(\mu_{\sigma}, s_{\sigma}^2),
$$

set by `settings$prior_sigmaF = c(mu, sd, use)`. Inside an MP with a short
rolling window (`nyrs = 5`), $\sigma_F$ is poorly determined by each cycle's
data. Estimating it in every fit has three costs:

1. one more, weakly identified parameter, so `nlminb()` needs more
   iterations and more restarts, and more fits end flagged as not converged
   (and are dropped, freezing the TAC);
2. the degree of smoothing changes from cycle to cycle and iteration to
   iteration, so part of the change in SPR seen by the HCR comes from the
   estimator rather than from the data;
3. the smoothing is less stable in exactly the years the HCR relies on, the
   last one or two years of the window.

A practical alternative is to estimate $\sigma_F$ once, in a conditioning
step on the historical sampled data with the full time series, and then
pass it to `flicc.sa()` with a tight prior, which holds it effectively
fixed:

```{r sigmaf}
# 1. conditioning fit: sigmaF estimated with the default prior
sigmaF_hat <- exp(fit$par$mpd[fit$par$par == "log_sigmaF"])
sigmaF_hat

# 2. fits with sigmaF held at the estimate (tight prior on log sigmaF)
settings_fix <- modifyList(settings,
                           list(prior_sigmaF = c(log(sigmaF_hat), 0.01, 1)))
t_fix <- system.time(
  fit_fix <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                    settings = settings_fix)
)[["elapsed"]]

rbind(estimated = c(time = t_fit, evals = fit$opt$evaluations[["function"]],
                    max_grad = fit$max_gradient,
                    SPR_last = tail(c(fit$report$spr), 1)),
      fixed     = c(time = t_fix, evals = fit_fix$opt$evaluations[["function"]],
                    max_grad = fit_fix$max_gradient,
                    SPR_last = tail(c(fit_fix$report$spr), 1)))
```

In the MSE, the conditioning step is done once per iteration on the
historical OEM samples (or once on the median), before `mp()` is called,
and the estimate is then passed in `flicc.sa(settings = ...)`. A per-iteration
value needs a small change in `flicc.sa()` (a vector of `sigmaF` by
iteration); with a single value it works with the current code.

Three cautions:

* The tight prior holds $\sigma_F$ close to the estimate but does not remove
  the parameter from the optimisation; a true fix through the TMB `map` is
  proposed in the developer notes.
* The gain in fit time is largest for short windows and noisy samples, where
  $\sigma_F$ is least identified; check it with the timing comparison above
  on the OM's own samples rather than assuming it.
* Do not set the prior mean to exactly `log(1) = 0`: `fiticc()` currently
  treats any element of `prior_sigmaF` equal to `FALSE` (i.e. 0) as "random
  walk off" (developer notes).

# Robustness options for repeated fits

An MP fits the model hundreds of times to data that nobody inspects. The
options below make the fits robust to the parts of a simulated length sample
that the model cannot explain. They are off by default in `fiticc()` and
are set through `flicc.sa(settings = ...)`.

## Tail cut of the growth-type groups: `maxsd`, `ngtg`, `tail_warning`

The GTG population model represents growth variation by `ngtg` growth
curves with Linf spread over $\pm$ `maxsd` standard deviations
($\sigma = CV_L L_\infty$). The truncation caps the largest length the model
can produce at $L_\infty (1 + \text{maxsd}\, CV_L)$ and makes the actual
spread smaller than `CVL` (about 0.9 CVL at `maxsd = 2`, the LBSPR default).
The OM, in contrast, typically samples lengths from a normal length-at-age
distribution up to 1.2 Linf or more. A few sampled fish beyond the largest
GTG Linf get near-zero probability and can drive CVL, selectivity and SPR.
`tail_warning = TRUE` reports how many observed fish fall in such bins
(useful when setting up the MP, not inside `mp()`); `maxsd = 3, ngtg = 19`
widens the reachable range and makes CVL close to the actual spread.

## Robust composition likelihood: `rob_eps`

`rob_eps` mixes the predicted proportions with a uniform,
$\tilde p_l = (1 - \varepsilon) p_l + \varepsilon / n_{bins}$, which bounds
the cost of a few fish in bins the model barely reaches. `rob_eps = 0.001`
is safe; 0.01 already changes selectivity and F with clean data.

## Plus group: `Lplus`

`Lplus` pools observed and predicted counts in all bins with lower bound
$\geq$ `Lplus` into one plus group before the likelihood (tail compression,
as in SS3). The likelihood then sees how many fish are at or above `Lplus`,
not how they fall into bins. Choose `Lplus` where counts become sparse,
typically near Linf. Negative log-likelihoods are comparable only between
fits with the same `Lplus`. Note that `LBIspr()` and `LBImean()` use the
unpooled observed compositions, so the indicators themselves are not
affected by `Lplus`, only the fit.

```{r robust}
fit_rob <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = modifyList(settings,
                                        list(Lplus = 50, rob_eps = 0.001)))
rbind(default = c(SPR = tail(c(fit$report$spr), 1),
                  LBIspr = sapply(LBIspr(fit), function(x) tail(c(index(x)), 1))),
      Lplus50_rob0.001 = c(SPR = tail(c(fit_rob$report$spr), 1),
                  LBIspr = sapply(LBIspr(fit_rob), function(x) tail(c(index(x)), 1))))
```

## Boundary fits and selectivity form

The SPR boundary check (`spr_max`) and the rescue refit (`refit_sel_fun`)
in `flicc.sa()` (Section 3.3) are the MP-level counterpart of these
likelihood options: they catch fits in which a dome-shaped selectivity
explains away the large fish. Both are cheap insurance. Together with the
tracked `used.est`, `sprbound.est` and `refit.est`, they show whether the
estimator is the weak point of an MP.

# Recommended starting values

| Element | Setting | Starting value |
|---|---|---|
| Data window | `nyrs` | 5 |
| Data weight | `ess.g` | 100–200 per gear |
| Model | `pop_model`, `obs_model` | `"gtg"`, `"dm"` |
| GTG | `ngtg`, `maxsd` | 13, 2 (or 19, 3 if large fish are common) |
| $\sigma_F$ | `prior_sigmaF` | estimated once, then `c(log(sigmaF_hat), 0.01, 1)` |
| Robustness | `Lplus`, `rob_eps` | near Linf, 0.001 |
| Reference | `spr`, `spr_ref`, `thresh` | 40, 40, 0.75 |
| Diagnostics | `drop_nonconv`, `spr_max`, `refit_sel_fun` | `TRUE`, 0.99, asymptotic forms |
| Optimiser | `n_restart`, `grad_tol` | 1, 1e-3 |
| HCR | `rfb.flicc.hcr()` | `index` = LBIspr of the gear selecting large fish, `f = NULL` or `"LBImean.<gear>"`, `spr_trigger` 0.25, `m` 0.95 |
| Limits | `flicc.is()` | `dtacupp = 1.2`, `dtaclow = 0.7` |

These are starting values for tuning, not recommendations for a particular
stock. The HCR triggers and the SPR safeguard in particular need to be
calibrated against the OM and tested across the robustness set.

# Appendix A: MP-related functions in FLicc

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `flicc.sa()` | `mp()` estimator: fits `fiticc()` per iteration, diagnostics, indicators |
| `lbi.hcr()` | `mp()` HCR: trend x SPR status, applied when both agree |
| `rfb.flicc.hcr()` | `mp()` HCR: $r^{\gamma} f b m$ (ICES rfb-type) |
| `flicc.is()` | `mp()` implementation system: TAC from multiplier, limits, area split |
| `LBIspr()` | proportion above $L_{ref}$ relative to the SPR target, by gear |
| `LBImean()` | mean length relative to Lmean(F = M) or Lmean($F_{SPR_x}$), by gear |
| `spr_rule()` | four-trigger SPR change multiplier |
| `r_rule()` | trend ratio of an index (`n1` over `n2`) |
| `hcr_sprlbi()` | `lbi.hcr()` logic for a single fit |
| `plot_hcrspr()` | plot of the SPR rule with status zones |
| `plot_LBIspr()`, `plot_LBIp()` | indicator and reference compositions |
| `fspr_flicc()`, `brp_tmb_flicc()`, `nf_flicc()` | $F_{SPR_x}$, per-recruit quantities and numbers-at-length (TMB) |
| `need_refit_flicc()`, `flicc_convergence()` | convergence checks |
| `lfdess()` | rescales compositions to an effective sample size |

# Appendix B: notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $s_g(l)$ | selectivity-at-length of gear $g$ |
| $N_l(F)$ | equilibrium numbers-at-length at apical F |
| $v_g(l)$ | $N_l(F_{SPR_x})\, s_g(l)$, vulnerable numbers at the target |
| $L_{ref,g}$ | length at which cumulative $v_g$ reaches `thresh` |
| $L_{c,g}$ | first length with $s_g(l) \geq 0.5$ |
| $\bar L^{ref}_g$ | reference mean length (F = M or $F_{SPR_x}$) |
| $F_{ap}$ | apical fishing mortality |
| $F_{SPR_x}$ | apical F giving SPR = x % |
| $Z^{rel}$ | $(F_{ap} + M)/(F_{SPR_x} + M)$ |
| $\sigma_F$ | standard deviation of the random walk on log F |
| $r, f, b, m$ | trend, fishing pressure, safeguard and precautionary components of the rfb rule |
